This guide describes how to add an external spatial method to the Giotto
Suite, either by reimplementing it natively or by connecting the original
tool. It reuses what the Suite already has: the five analysis verbs and their
`Param` classes, the setters for every slot, the analysis history, and
`package_check()` for tools that are installed only when used. No method needs
its own package, and nothing is installed for users who never run it.

# Two kinds of integration

- **A native reimplementation** recomputes a published method with Suite
  code, for example the BANKSY embedding (`runNeighborhoodPCA()`) or HMRF
  (`runHMRF()`). It lives in **Giotto**. A small engine with no Giotto
  dependency can be its own package that Giotto suggests, as `spatialHMRF`
  and `spatialDWLS` are.
- **A connection** runs the original tool and moves data in and out, for
  example ONTraC (Python) or CellChat (R). It lives in **GiottoConnect**, one
  file per tool: `R/tool-<name>.R`.

# Reuse before writing

Build on what the Suite already has and write only what is specific to the
method. Spatial neighbours come from a stored spatial network
(`createSpatialNetwork()`), PCA from `reduceData(x, pcaParam())`, clustering
from the existing clustering functions. BANKSY's native embedding adds only
its neighbour weights and gradient (`neighborhood_operators()`) on top of a
stored kNN network. If an existing building block is too slow for the new
method, improve it there rather than working around it.

# Verbs return, wrappers write

Each method is a `Param` class plus a method on one of the five verbs, chosen
by what it returns:

| Verb | Returns |
|---|---|
| `processData()` | values of the same shape (normalized, smoothed) |
| `filterData()` | the IDs to keep |
| `reduceData()` | an embedding or decomposition |
| `clusterData()` | one label per cell |
| `analyzeData()` | statistics and other outputs |

The method on a data class (a matrix, a table) returns what its verb
promises and never touches a giotto object. A thin `run<Name>()` wrapper
reads the inputs from the giotto object, calls the verb, and writes the
result with the existing setters.

# Where results go

Results go into the slots that already exist:

| Output | Slot | Written with |
|---|---|---|
| a label or value per cell | cell metadata | `addCellMetadata()` |
| a value per feature | feature metadata | `addFeatMetadata()` |
| cells x dimensions | dimension reduction | `createDimObj()` + `setDimReduction()` |
| cells x categories (proportions, probabilities) | spatial enrichment | `createSpatEnrObj()` + `setSpatialEnrichment()` |
| features x cells values | expression | `setExpression()` |
| a graph on expression or an embedding | nearest-neighbour network | `setNearestNetwork()` |
| a spatial graph | spatial network | `setSpatialNetwork()` |
| anything else (interaction tables, fitted models, tool objects) | none | returned to the caller |

# Plots

Results in existing slots can be drawn with existing plots, so most
integrations need none of their own. ONTraC is the example: niche clusters
with `spatPlot2D(cell_color = )`, their probabilities with
`spatCellPlot2D(spat_enr_names = )`, NT scores per cell type with
`ridgePlot(group_by = )`, and cell type composition with
`plotLabelComposition()`. List these in the wrapper's help page.

When a tool has a view no Giotto plot covers, and that view only makes sense
for this tool, add one plot function to the tool's file:

- name it `plot<Tool><What>()`, as `plotONTraCConnectivity()` (the graph of
  ONTraC's niche clusters);
- read what it draws from the slots the wrapper wrote (for ONTraC, the
  spatial enrichment's `misc`), never from the tool's output files;
- put `ggplot2` (and any other plotting package) in `Suggests`, check it with
  `package_check()`, and return through
  `GiottoVisuals::plot_output_handler()` so `show_plot`, `return_plot` and
  `save_plot` work as in the other Giotto plots.

A view that several tools would use belongs in GiottoVisuals instead.

# Recording what was run

The wrapper ends with

```{r, eval=FALSE}
update_giotto_params(gobject, description = "_<name>",
    attachments = list(param = param))
```

so the analysis history keeps the `Param` with its settings. A `Param` holds
settings only, never data.

# Dependencies

- The tool is never in `Imports`. It goes in `Suggests` (CRAN,
  Bioconductor), or in `Remotes` plus an install hint for GitHub-only tools,
  and is checked with `package_check()` when the function runs. Call
  functions of a GitHub-only tool with `getExportedValue()` so `R CMD check`
  stays clean.
- Python tools get their environment when first run, with
  `reticulate::py_require()` (reticulate >= 1.41). Pin the tool's version.
- Tests use `skip_if_not_installed()`, so a broken tool release breaks only
  its own function.
- A function shared with another package is exported as a documented
  `snake_case` utility, not reached with `:::`.

# Names and credit

- The `Param` class is named after the method: `ontracParam`,
  `cellchatParam`. A connection's wrapper is `run<Tool>()`.
- A native reimplementation gets a descriptive name, not the tool's, so a
  wrapper of the original can sit beside it: `runNeighborhoodPCA()` next to
  `GiottoConnect::runBanksy()`.
- Its help page names the original method and paper under `@references`,
  asks users to cite it, and says how it differs from the original and how
  closely it matches.

# Checking an integration

- Compare against the original tool on the same input, with a seed, and keep
  the comparison script outside the package (for example in
  `examples/<tool>_comparison/`).
- `GiottoConnect::checkGiottoMethod()` (and `expect_giotto_method()` in
  tests) checks a wrapper against these rules: which slots it wrote, that
  the history holds its `Param`, and that its help page has references.
- Templates for both kinds are in GiottoConnect's
  `giotto-integrate-tool` skill.
